desc:
The dots of an IPv4 address were erased, leaving only a string of digits. Insert exactly three dots into digits (never changing the order of the digits and never dropping one) to rebuild every valid IPv4 address.

An address has four parts. Each part is a decimal number from 0 to 255 written without leading zeros (the part 0 is fine, but 01 or 00 are not).

Return each valid address as a row of its four numbers, for example [255, 255, 11, 135]. Rows may be in any order.
constraints: digits consists only of the characters 0-9
hints: You must choose where the three dots go, so choose the four parts one after another. How long can a part be?
A part has 1 to 3 digits. Try each length, reject it if it is longer than 1 digit and starts with 0, or if its value is above 255, and recurse for the next part.
Prune with lengths: after choosing some parts, the remaining digits must fit the remaining parts, which need between 1 and 3 digits each. The whole string has to be used exactly.
editorial: Recurse on the start index of the next part and the parts chosen so far. When four parts are placed, accept only if the whole string has been used. Otherwise try part lengths 1, 2 and 3: stop trying longer lengths as soon as the part would run past the end of the string, starts with 0 and has more than one digit, or has a value above 255.

A simple length check prunes most dead branches early: with r parts still to place and m digits left, you need r ≤ m ≤ 3r. There are at most 34 = 81 ways to pick the four lengths, so the search is constant time, O(1), for any input.
Because a part has no leading zeros, the numeric row identifies the written address uniquely, so no two rows are equal.
